title: When Your Case Needs Two Experts Instead of One
description: Scoping a case for one expert when it needs two is the most expensive expert mistake. Here's how to spot the split before disclosure.
keywords: medical causation vs medical billing expert
fire origin and cause vs engineering expert

blocks.text: The most expensive expert mistake is not hiring the wrong person. It is scoping a case for one expert when it actually requires two, and discovering that after disclosure.
The second retention then happens on a compressed timeline, at a premium, with less choice of candidate. Recognizing the split early costs nothing.
The Basic Test
Ask what opinions the case actually requires, then ask whether one discipline covers all of them.
Not one person, one discipline. An expert can be brilliant and still be offering an opinion outside their field, which is a qualification problem regardless of how capable they are.
The Common Splits
Liability and damages. These are almost always different experts. The engineer who explains how a product failed does not calculate lost earnings. Attorneys generally get this one right.

Two liability disciplines in one incident. Harder to spot. A premises case involving both a property's security protocol and its management practices touches two distinct fields. A fire case may need origin and cause separated from the engineering analysis of what ignited. A construction case may need design separated from installation.

Medical causation and medical billing. Whether an injury was caused by the incident and whether the treatment charges were reasonable and necessary are different questions answered by different people.

Treating physician and retained expert. A treating physician can testify about their own treatment. Opinions extending into causation, permanency, or future care usually call for a retained expert with a full report.

Standard of care across specialties. A malpractice case involving multiple providers in different specialties frequently needs an expert per specialty, because the standard of care is specialty-specific.
Why Attorneys Consolidate
Usually cost. Sometimes the belief that fewer experts means a simpler story for the jury.

Both are reasonable instincts and both can backfire. A single expert stretched across two disciplines invites a qualification challenge on the weaker half. Losing that opinion mid-case is more expensive than the second expert would have been.

There is also a version where consolidation is correct. Some experts genuinely hold dual qualifications, and where one person credibly covers both fields, using them is cleaner and cheaper. The distinction is whether the dual qualification is real and documented, or whether you are hoping it holds.
Spotting the Split Early
Work backward from the opinions you need at trial.
Write out every proposition an expert will have to establish. Then, for each one, name the discipline that owns it. Where two different disciplines appear, you likely have two experts.
The exercise takes fifteen minutes and it happens before you have spent anything.
The Cost Question, Honestly
Two experts cost more than one. That is real, particularly in cases where the exposure does not obviously justify it.

But the comparison is not two experts versus one. It is two experts retained deliberately versus one expert plus a second retained under deadline pressure after a qualification problem surfaces, plus the motion practice in between.
Where budget genuinely constrains the case, the better move is often narrowing what you ask the single expert to cover rather than stretching them across both.
What This Means for the Search

If a case needs two experts, the search should account for that from the start. Sourcing them together means you can check for consistency between the two opinions and confirm neither has a conflict with the other's prior work.
Fee structures differ by discipline, so it also means you can budget the whole engagement rather than discovering the second expert's rates after committing to the first.

The Bottom Line

Scope by opinion, not by person. Write out what each expert has to establish and name the discipline that owns each one. Where two disciplines appear, plan for two experts from the start, because the alternative is finding out on a deadline.
